content.text:
I'm treating each cell block as a node in a graph, with gaps in walls acting as connections between adjacent blocks. The largest connected component of blocks gets labeled 4, while isolated blocks get labeled 3 — and I'm verifying this against example 1, where a gap cell connects two blocks and correctly receives a 4.

Now I'm confirming the rule holds: any block with at least one gap in its walls gets 4, otherwise 3. Checking this against example 2 as well, then mapping out the block structure for the actual test grid, which has a 27x27 layout with walls at rows and columns 3, 7, 11, 15, 19, 23.

I'm scanning through each wall row and column for gaps (zeros) that would connect adjacent blocks, noting connections like (R0,C1)-(R0,C2) from a gap at row2 col7, and tracking zeros appearing at wall row3 near columns 6-7 and 26.

Continuing to trace wall gaps row by row, mapping which grid cells connect to each other based on where the zeros appear in each wall row.

Continuing to trace wall gaps row by row, mapping zero positions to connections between grid cells across rows 16 through 21.

Continuing down: row24 gives a gap at (R6,C2)-(R6,C3), row25 at (R6,C0)-(R6,C1), and row26 gives gaps at (R6,C1)-(R6,C2) and (R6,C3)-(R6,C4). Now I'm going through each block to mark which have a gap on any side (making them width 4) versus none (width 3) - row0 has C1,C2,C6 as 4 and the rest as 3, row1 has C0-C4 and C6 as 4 with only C5 as 3, and I'm starting the same check for row2.

Now I'm assembling the actual grid, keeping wall cells at value 5 except where gaps punch through to become 4, and writing out row0's specific numeric sequence.

Continuing to fill in rows 2 through 5 with their gap adjustments...

Still mapping out the maze grid rows...

Still mapping out the maze grid rows...

Continuing to work through rows 22-25 of the grid, tracking zero positions at specific columns and converting them to wall values while filling the rest with the row's base pattern.
